snippet.title: The US can hit any target on Earth in under 60 minutes. No nukes needed. #military #usa
snippet.description:

The Tomahawk cruise missile launches from submarines, flies 1,500 miles at 100 feet altitude, and can change its target mid-flight. Over 140 US ships and submarines carry Tomahawks. In February 2026 the US demonstrated this by striking targets across dozens of Iranian cities from ships, planes, and bases in multiple countries simultaneously. The US defense budget is $961 billion a year. More than the next 10 countries combined.

snippet.title: Hollywood Lied About Egyptian Pyramids For Decades.
snippet.description:
In 1990, a horse accidentally stumbled near the Giza plateau and revealed hidden burial shafts that changed everything we thought we knew about the pyramids. Archaeologists led by Egypt's own archaeology chief Zahi Hawass excavated the tombs and found the skeletons of pyramid builders buried with jars of beer and bread for the afterlife, an honor only given to respected Egyptians. No slave in ancient Egypt was ever buried near a pharaoh. The workers lived in an organized city with bakeries, breweries, and medical facilities. 

10,000 workers received 21 cattle and 23 sheep every single day. They worked 3-month rotating paid shifts and their remains show arthritis and spinal injuries from decades of hard but honored labor. The slavery myth was popularized centuries later with zero archaeological backing. The tombs exist. The records exist. The proof has been sitting in the sand the whole time.

Everyone thinks slaves built the pyramids. The archaeology says otherwise. 

✅ Workers were PAID in bread, beer & medical care
✅ Graffiti found ON-SITE reads: "Friends of Khufu" — a proud work crew name
✅ Worker villages had bakeries, breweries & field hospitals
✅ Skeletons show healed fractures — proof of medical treatment
✅ Overseers were buried WITH HONOR near the pyramids

The slave narrative started with Herodotus in 450 BC — 
2,000 years AFTER the pyramids were built. He wasn't even there.

snippet.title: 6th Largest Economy?! The Real Story Behind India's Ranking #Economy #India #Facts
snippet.description:
India is now ranked as the 6th largest economy in the world—but is this really a setback?

According to the IMF World Economic Outlook 2026, India’s GDP stands at around $4.15 trillion, slightly behind the UK ($4.27T) and Japan ($4.38T). This shift has raised concerns, but the reality is very different.

This change is not due to economic weakness. Instead, it’s driven by:

Revised GDP calculations
Rupee weakening against the US Dollar
Global rankings based on dollar terms

The bigger picture? Most major economies beyond the top ranks are clustered around the $4 trillion mark, meaning even small changes can impact rankings.

The good news: IMF projections suggest India could rise to the top 4 by 2027 and even break into the top 3 by 2031.

So is this a decline—or just a temporary shift in numbers? Watch to understand the real story behind India's economic growth.

snippet.title: Why Noida Factory Workers Are Protesting | The Reality Every Salaried Indian Must Face
snippet.description:
Thousands of factory workers in Noida have taken to the streets — and their struggle reflects a deeper issue affecting every salaried Indian.

With wages barely increasing and the cost of living rising sharply, workers are finding it harder to survive. While states like Haryana have raised minimum wages significantly, Uttar Pradesh hasn’t revised wages since 2012.

Between 2021 and 2026, inflation surged by around 25%, but wages only increased by about 20%. Essentials like LPG, rent, and food have become expensive, pushing many to extreme measures just to make ends meet.

The new Labour Codes were expected to bring relief — but unclear rules and implementation gaps have only added to confusion, often leading to longer working hours instead of better conditions.

So the big question is:
Are labour reforms actually helping workers — or making things worse?

Watch till the end and share your thoughts in the comments.

snippet.title: Can AI help you change the world? | Creating Change Through Social Entrepreneurship
snippet.description:
Yale's Teresa Chahine on how AI is reshaping social entrepreneurship, joined by two founders building real ventures with it.

Teresa Chahine reflects on how her thinking has shifted over eight years at Yale: away from the solo "hero entrepreneur" and toward collective action, social movements, and indigenous wisdom. 

She's then joined by Bhavya Chauhan, founder of HAVN, and Belabbes Benkredda, who is building a venture focused on the health of public spheres. Bhavya shares how she used vibe coding with Cursor and Claude to build and test an MVP, and how HAVN moved from prototype to piloting. Belabbes lays out his theory of a "fourth wave" of AI-driven public spheres. Both founders weigh the promise and the risks of AI, and return to one idea: technology should strengthen human relationships, not replace them.

Community Notes on X started with a wild idea: Instead of tech companies deciding what's true, what if you let people fact-check each other? Jay Baxter and Keith Coleman, who helped build the crowdsourced system adding context to misleading posts, discuss how the program reduces viral misinformation — and why people across the political spectrum trust it. In conversation with TED guest curator Audrey Tang, they discuss how their "surprising agreement" algorithm could reveal the common ground that quietly exists across a polarized internet. (Followed by a note from TED guest curators Divya Siddarth and Audrey Tang) (Recorded at TED2026 on April 14, 2026)

snippet.title: New Public Management Explained | How Government Became More Business-Like
snippet.description:
New Public Management is an approach that introduced private-sector methods into government organisations.

It focuses on efficiency, performance targets, competition, outsourcing, cost control, and customer-focused services.

In this video, we explain its main features, advantages, criticisms, and impact on public administration.

What You’ll Learn
• what New Public Management means
• why governments adopted it
• its main features
• its advantages and weaknesses
• why public services cannot be run exactly like businesses

What Is New Public Management?
New Public Management, often called NPM, became influential during the 1980s and 1990s.
It aimed to reduce traditional bureaucracy and improve public-sector performance.
Instead of focusing only on rules and procedures, organisations were encouraged to focus on results.

The main question became:
What outcomes is the organisation actually producing?
Main Features
New Public Management includes:
• performance targets
• measurable results
• competition
• outsourcing
• cost reduction
• managerial freedom
• customer-focused services
• private-sector practices

Managers were given more responsibility for achieving results.

Why Governments Adopted It
Governments adopted NPM because traditional public organisations were often criticised for being:
• slow
• expensive
• rigid
• inefficient
• difficult to measure
• unresponsive to citizens
NPM promised better services with fewer resources.

Citizens as Customers
One major idea was to treat citizens more like customers.
Government departments were encouraged to improve:
• service speed
• communication
• convenience
• accessibility
• complaint handling
• user satisfaction
This helped public organisations pay more attention to service quality.
However, citizens are not simply customers.
They also have rights, responsibilities, and different levels of need.

Competition and Outsourcing
NPM encouraged governments to introduce competition.
Some services were outsourced to private companies.
Examples may include:
• waste collection
• transport services
• maintenance
• technology support
• cleaning services
The goal was to reduce costs and improve performance.
But outsourcing can also create problems if private profit becomes more important than service quality.

Performance Measurement
Public organisations were encouraged to use:
• targets
• key performance indicators
• audits
• rankings
• service standards
• financial reports

Measurement can improve accountability.
But poor targets may encourage employees to focus on numbers instead of real public outcomes.
Simple Example
Imagine a government hospital wants to reduce waiting times.
Under New Public Management, managers may:
• set waiting-time targets
• measure staff performance
• compare hospitals
• outsource some services
• publish results
• reward better performance
This may improve efficiency.
But if staff focus only on meeting the target, the quality of patient care may suffer.

Advantages
New Public Management can provide:
• clearer goals
• improved efficiency
• stronger accountability
• better service quality
• cost awareness
• faster decisions
• greater managerial responsibility
It pushed public organisations to show actual results.

Disadvantages
NPM can also create:
• too much focus on cost
• pressure to meet targets
• weaker public accountability
• poor-quality outsourcing
• short-term decision-making
• unfair treatment of vulnerable citizens
• confusion between public service and profit
Efficiency matters, but it is not the only goal of government.

Reality Check
New Public Management improved performance in some areas.
But it also created new problems.
Government services cannot always be judged using profit, speed, or customer satisfaction alone.

And here is the brutal truth:
A public service may be efficient and still be unfair.
Government must balance performance with equality, accountability, and public interest.

Why This Matters
Understanding NPM explains:
• why governments use performance targets
• why public services are outsourced
• why citizens are treated like customers
• why managers have more responsibility
• why efficiency can conflict with fairness

Because at the end:
New Public Management tried to make government work more like business, but public service must remain focused on citizens—not profit.

snippet.title: Public Administration vs Public Policy | Key Differences Explained
snippet.description:
Public policy and public administration are closely connected, but they perform different roles in government.

Public policy focuses on deciding what problems government should address and what actions should be taken. Public administration focuses on implementing those decisions through departments, budgets, employees, and public services.

In this video, we explain the main differences between public administration and public policy using simple examples.

What You’ll Learn
• what public policy means
• what public administration means
• how policy decisions are created
• how administrators implement policies
• why both fields depend on each other

What Is Public Policy?
Public policy refers to the decisions and actions taken by governments to address public problems.

It may focus on areas such as:
• education
• healthcare
• taxation
• employment
• housing
• transport
• crime
• environmental protection

Public policy answers questions such as:
What problem should government solve?

What action should government take?

Who should benefit from the policy?

What Is Public Administration?

Public administration focuses on managing government organisations and implementing public policies.

It includes:
• managing public employees
• preparing budgets
• delivering government services
• applying laws and regulations
• maintaining public records
• monitoring programmes
• communicating with citizens

Public administration answers a different question:
How will the government turn this policy into practical results?

The Main Difference

The simplest difference is:

Public policy decides what should be done.

Public administration decides how it will be done.

Policy is mainly concerned with goals and decisions.

Administration is mainly concerned with implementation and management.

However, the boundary is not always clear because administrators can also influence policy through advice, research, experience, and feedback.

Simple Example
Imagine the government decides that every child should receive free primary education.

That decision is public policy.

Public administrators must then:
• build and maintain schools
• hire and train teachers
• distribute textbooks
• prepare education budgets
• monitor attendance
• manage school records
• evaluate results

The policy creates the promise.

Administration turns that promise into an actual public service.

Who Is Involved?
Public policy may involve:
• elected politicians
• ministers
• legislators
• policy advisers
• researchers
• interest groups
• members of the public

Public administration mainly involves:
• civil servants
• government managers
• local authorities
• public agencies
• programme officers
• frontline public employees

Politicians usually set the overall direction.

Administrators manage the systems required to achieve it.

Policy Formulation vs Implementation

Public policy usually includes:
• identifying a public problem
• studying possible solutions
• selecting an approach
• creating laws or programmes
• setting goals and priorities

Public administration usually includes:
• allocating resources
• assigning responsibilities
• creating procedures
• delivering services
• monitoring performance
• reporting results

Policy formulation and implementation must work together.

A weak policy cannot be rescued easily by good administration.

And a strong policy can still fail because of poor implementation.

Key Differences
Public policy focuses more on:
• public problems
• political priorities
• laws and decisions
• long-term goals
• policy alternatives

Public administration focuses more on:
• organisations
• employees
• budgets
• procedures
• service delivery
• implementation

Policy asks what government should achieve.

Administration asks how government can achieve it efficiently and fairly.

Why This Matters
Understanding the difference helps explain:
• how government decisions are made
• why policies sometimes fail
• what civil servants actually do
• why implementation requires resources
• how politics connects with management
• why policy evaluation matters

Because at the end:
Public policy provides the direction, while public administration turns that direction into action.

snippet.title: How Malaysia is looking to seize its upstream opportunity with Petronas SVP Datuk Bacho Pilong
snippet.description:
Let’s Talk Energy with Datuk Bacho Pilong, Senior Vice President at Petronas and head of Malaysia Petroleum Management, the Southeast Asian nation’s upstream regulator. Malaysia is a long-time oil producer and is currently the world’s fifth-largest LNG exporter, providing crucial supply diversification for gas importers in the region. At the same time, the country’s own energy needs are growing rapidly as its economy matures, requiring new fields and further investment to keep both its domestic market and its international customers well supplied. Pilong’s task has taken on greater urgency following the war in the Middle East, which has caused energy importers including Malaysia to re-emphasize domestic supplies and has brought renewed interest from international companies looking to manage growing supply risks through greater geographic diversity in their portfolios.  

+ What are Malaysia’s goals for its upstream sector and what are its strategies to achieve them?
+ How is the nation’s latest bid round progressing and what is the outlook for international investments?
+ What will be the impact of the war in the Middle East on interest and activity in Malaysia’s upstream sector?

snippet.title: E-Governance and Digital Government Explained
snippet.description:
E-governance uses digital technology to improve government services and communication with citizens.

In this video, we explain online public services, digital records, transparency, efficiency, and the main risks of digital government.

What You’ll Learn
• what e-governance means
• how digital services help citizens
• what risks digital government creates

What Is E-Governance?
E-governance means using technology to improve how government operates.

It may include:
• online service portals
• digital records
• mobile government applications

It connects citizens with government more quickly.

Digital Government Services
Citizens may use digital systems to:
• pay taxes or bills
• apply for licences
• access public records

This reduces paperwork, travel, and waiting times.

Benefits of E-Governance
Digital government can improve:
• speed and convenience
• transparency
• service accessibility

It can also reduce administrative costs.

Simple Example
Imagine someone needs to renew a government licence.
Instead of visiting an office, they can:
• submit documents online
• pay digitally
• track the application

This makes the process faster and easier.

Transparency and Participation
Technology can help governments publish:
• budgets and reports
• public decisions
• service performance

Citizens can also submit complaints or feedback online.

Main Risks
Digital government can create problems such as:
• cyberattacks
• loss of privacy
• digital exclusion

People without internet access or digital skills may be left behind.

Artificial Intelligence in Government
Governments may use AI to:
• answer citizen questions
• analyse public data
• automate routine services

But automated decisions still require human review and accountability.

Reality Check
Moving a weak government process online does not automatically improve it.
A confusing paper system can become a confusing digital system.

The brutal truth is:
Digital government only works when technology improves the service instead of simply hiding bureaucracy behind a screen.

Why This Matters
Understanding e-governance explains:
• why services are moving online
• how technology can improve access
• why privacy and cybersecurity matter

Because at the end:
E-governance should make government more accessible, transparent, and responsive to citizens.

snippet.title: The Man Who Survived Both Atomic Bombs
snippet.description:
On August 6, 1945, a nuclear bomb destroyed Hiroshima.
Three days later, another bomb fell on Nagasaki.

One man experienced both.

Tsutomu Yamaguchi survived the first explosion in Hiroshima, traveled home to Nagasaki the next day, and then witnessed the second atomic bomb detonate just miles away.

Against impossible odds, he lived through both nuclear attacks and later spent his life speaking about nuclear weapons and peace.

This is one of the most unbelievable survival stories in modern history.

snippet.title: Decentralisation and Local Government Explained
snippet.description:
Decentralisation means transferring authority and responsibility from central government to regional or local governments.

In this video, we explain how local government works, why decentralisation matters, and the risks of weak funding or accountability.

What You’ll Learn
• what decentralisation means
• what local governments do
• why local decision-making matters

What Is Decentralisation?
Decentralisation transfers:
• decision-making power
• financial resources
• service responsibilities

The goal is to bring government closer to citizens.

What Is Local Government?
Local government manages public services within a city, district, or community.
It may oversee:
• waste collection
• local roads
• parks and planning

Its responsibilities vary between countries.

Why Decentralise Power?
Local authorities often understand community needs better than central government.
Decentralisation can improve:
• faster decisions
• citizen participation
• locally designed services

This can make public services more relevant.

Simple Example
Imagine a town has serious waste-management problems.
A local council can respond faster by changing collection schedules, hiring workers, or improving recycling.
A distant central ministry may not understand the problem as clearly.

Financial Decentralisation
Local governments need money to perform their duties.
Funding may come from:
• local taxes
• service fees
• central government grants

Responsibility without funding usually leads to failure.

Advantages
Decentralisation can create:
• stronger local accountability
• faster service delivery
• more citizen involvement

It can also encourage local innovation.
Common Problems
Decentralisation may fail because of:
• weak local capacity
• corruption
• unequal resources between regions

Poorer areas may struggle to provide the same service quality as wealthier ones.

Reality Check
Giving power to local government does not automatically improve services.
Local authorities also need skilled staff, funding, clear powers, and public oversight.

The brutal truth is:
Decentralisation without resources is not real decentralisation—it is simply passing responsibility downward.

Why This Matters
Understanding decentralisation explains:
• why local councils exist
• why services differ between regions
• why local accountability matters

Because at the end:
Central government sets national direction, while local government turns many decisions into community-level services.

snippet.title: Man Struck by Lightning 7 TIMES and Survived
snippet.description:
Between 1942 and 1977, Virginia park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning 7 times. It set his hair on fire 3 times. He carried a can of water everywhere just to put out his own head. He holds the Guinness World Record to this day.

USAF., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

snippet.title: Purpose and Values in Teams | Connected Leadership with Peter Boyd
snippet.description:
A clear team purpose acts as a North Star that guides decisions, builds trust, and empowers distributed teams. This lesson walks through the strategy pyramid and offers practical guidance for crafting vision and mission statements that actually drive behavior.

Key topics:
- Why team purpose matters: direction, motivation, and coordination
- The role of shared values and the tension with diversity
- The strategy pyramid: vision, mission, values, and strategy
- Crafting concise, memorable vision and mission statements
- Researching real-world examples and reflecting on fit
- McKinsey data on the gap between mission and impact

📚 About the Course:

This course is designed to maximize your ability to create change at the individual, team and system levels. Through study, reflection, and deploying practical tools, you will establish a firm connection between your clearly articulated Purpose, effective Priorities, visualized Potential for success, and pathway to maximized Progress. But, what does that mean in practice?

When you take this course, you will:

Improve your ability to get the most out of life: Learn a simple practice to reflect on your purpose, clarify priorities, visualize your potential, and maximize your effectiveness at progressing towards your goals.

Strengthen your leadership toolkit: Tap into your unique leadership style and strengths and join or create a community of others to maximize your potential as a team.

Create change through systems thinking: Become a more effective agent of positive change and appreciate the power and complexity of system thinking.

Course Takeaways:
Improve your ability to get the most out of life
Strengthen your leadership toolkit
Practice and apply systems thinking to plan for change

snippet.title: What was your favorite toy growing up? #TEDTalks
snippet.description: What was your favorite toy when you were a kid? Your answer might reveal more about you than you expect, says toy historian Chris Byrne. From Matchbox cars and Barbie to Rubik's Cube and Squishmallows, he explores how playthings reflect cultural values and influence who you become as an adult.
